newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah shows upward bias post-poll.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah shows upward bias post-poll.

text.p: * Indonesian rupiah steady but showing firm bias as early election results within market expectations.
* Thai baht firms offshore as players sell dollars to cover their positions in face of continued central bank ban on lending by domestic banks.
* Malaysian ringgit shows signs of firming after news of an 8.2 percent rise in first quarter GDP.
* Singapore dollar off lows as early ringgit/Sing buying fades.

The Indonesian rupiah showed a firm bias in Friday morning trade as initial results from the country's general election indicated the ruling Golkar party would win its projected majority, dealers said.
"The results appear to be within expectations," a Japanese bank dealer in Jakarta said.
Dealers said the results, showing the Golkar taking an unassailable lead with more than half the potential ballots counted, should restore calm to the market.
Spot rupiah was quoted at 2,436.5/38.5 at 0425 gmt compared with an opening of 2,441.00/43.00.
"I think the rupiah is likely to strengthen further when more election results come in, confirming the current trend," the Japanese bank dealer said.

Another dealer said THursday's rally on the Jakarta stock market seemed to have encouraged rupiah investors, though some remained cautious about possible social unrest in the aftermath of the election.
"I favour selling the dollar around 2,444.0/45.0 for it to go back down to the 2,435.0 region," a Singapore dealer said.
The Thai baht firmed in offshore markets as players were forced to sell their dollar holdings to acquire baht in the face of the central bank's continued ban on offshore lending by domestic banks.
The baht was quoted at 25.130/25.150 to the dollar at 0425 GMT against 25.600/25.640 baht late Thursday.
Onshore, the baht was traded around 25.825/25.835 to the dollar compared with 25.830/25.850 late Thursday.
The Bank of Thailand (BOT) fixed the mid-rate at 25.80 baht against 25.75 on Thurday.

"For offshore speculators without what the central bank termed as 'reasonable underlying transactions', selling dollars is the most sensible option now to get the baht to cover their positions," a U.S. bank dealer in Bangkok said.
"If you borrow onshore baht, that would cost you around 1,000 percent in interest rate for overnight borrowing," he added.
The demand for baht drove the swap premium for one-month tenor up to 82/100 satangs per dollar in the offshore market compared with 40/60 satangs earlier.
"When you borrow from the swap market at that rate, the implied interest is only around 40 percent, much better than borrowing from onshore," another dealer said.
In Malaysia, the ringgit showed signs of strengthening after the lunch-time release of first quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) data.
Bank Negara said Malaysia's GDP grew 8.2 percent in the first quarter of 1997, against 8.3 percent in the same period last year.
MMS Standard & Poor's said in a market commentary that the market had discounted a figure of between 7.8-8.2 percent.
The ringgit had come under pressure earlier on rumours of weak data and stop-loss dollar buying around the 2.5110/20 levels.
But dealers said the dollar's upside was capped by caution ahead of the data and wariness after a U.S. fund sold about $200 million around 2.5140/50 ringgit on Thursday.
"I would be a buyer of the dollar on dips to 2.5050 and below if it goes down there," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. The ringgit was quoted at 2.5133/43 to the dollar at 0425 GMT.
The Singapore dollar remained lethargic but recovered from its early lows against the U.S. dollar as early buying of the ringgit/Sing cross faded.
"Dollar/Sing should trade in a range but it's looking a tad heavy around 1.4315/20," the European bank dealer said.
-- Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221 384-6364), Anchalee Koetsawang in Bangkok (662) 652-0642 and Sonali Desai in Singapore (65-8703090)
